title: Spiral galaxy M81
caption: The spiral galaxy M81, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M81 · constellation Ursa Major · about 11 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, A. Zezas (CfA), and A. Filippenko (UC Berkeley) Acknowledgment: Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA) & O. Fox (University of California, Berkeley)

recognition.text: Ranked #92 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble photo shows the spiral galaxy M81, about 11 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. It was recorded with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters.

Somewhere within it lies supernova 1993J. Astronomers found that this exploded star had a companion star that had stayed hidden in the supernova's glare for 21 years. An annotated version of the image marks the spot where the supernova sits.

A supernova is the explosive death of a star, bright enough for a while to be seen across intergalactic distances. Its glow can easily outshine a neighboring star, which is how the companion of supernova 1993J could stay hidden for so long before astronomers finally picked it out.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (8.80 x 6.02 arcminutes) and distance (11 million light years), the frame spans roughly 28,000 × 19,000 light-years. Its light set out about 11 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and near-infrared light reveal detail the eye can't see.
